Okay, that's a whole separate issue, but I'll take a crack at it.

Starting with your last question, because it's the most important in this context. Basically, the Earth is massive and that makes the resulting gravity well absurdly strong, and you're underestimating how strong that pull is on everything inside the well. Imagine space as a blanket stretched taught corner to corner. The more massive an object is, the bigger the depression it creates on the blanket when you put it down. The depression of space around that massive object is gravity - anything trying to escape from that gravity needs to be able to "roll up the hill" as it were, and the "hill" for celestial bodies is ridiculously steep. We represent this with our standard gravitational acceleration here on earth as "10 m/s^2 downwards" acceleration. This is what you need to overcome if you want to get up the hill. Now, what does this mean for matter? Well, If you're an American who likes Cars, that's a 0-60 time of 2.8 seconds for any object on Earth, directly towards the Earth's center of mass. That hill is incredibly steep - So Steep that matter on Earth typically can't escape from it. Consequently, every substance on Earth, be it Solid, Liquid or Gas, is in a perpetual state of freefall towards Earth's center of mass. To summarize, Earth is so massive that the Gravitational force is really, REALLY strong. We don't feel it because we're used to it, just like we're used to having about a metric ton of atmosphere sitting on top of us at any given moment, but it's definitely there.

Moving along to the question of how something small and weak can defy it - It's not actually defying it. It's abusing how the system works in order to achieve what we want. Without going into too much detail on this second part (because flight dynamics are pretty complicated), essentially in order to get off the ground, aircraft utilize the properties of air to generate lift. Basically imagine the wings of a plane or the blades of a helicopter as a gigantic set of oars. The flat bottom gets pulled through the surrounding air at high speed, and gets pushed up, whereas the curved top with limited air contact tapers in towards the back and the air behind pushes down on it. Overall, doing this fast enough and displacing enough air results in an overall upwards force, allowing an aircraft to fly. If you'd like to know more about this for helicopters, this guy has a really good video series on the topic, and explains things way better than me.
